overview: This single-page Department of State list of papers inventories correspondence concerning disabled or wrecked Japanese vessels, chiefly the sinking of the passenger steamer SUNKI MARU by a mine near White Tiger Hill, downriver from Hankow, and arrangements for returning the rescued crew of the wrecked fishing boat DAICHI SAIHO MARU. The indexed communications trace negotiations among the State Department, Navy Department, U.S. Embassy in Tokyo, Japanese Foreign Office, Guam authorities, and USS PENGUIN over whether survivors should be delivered at Saipan, Guam, or Rota. The sheet records casualties in the SUNKI MARU sinking and notes that no American or other Occidental passengers were aboard.

subfiles.title: List of papers on disabled, wrecked, and stranded Japanese merchant vessels
subfiles.about: An index summarizes telegrams and memoranda concerning the mined passenger steamer SUNKI MARU and the return of survivors from the wrecked fishing boat DAICHI SAIHO MARU.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records that SUNKI MARU sank after striking a mine near White Tiger Hill, 28 miles downriver from Hankow, killing three Chinese and twenty Japanese, with no American or other Occidental travelers aboard. Most entries concern efforts to return the rescued crew of DAICHI SAIHO MARU using USS PENGUIN, including requests to visit Saipan and later proposals for a transfer at Guam or Rota. The Japanese Foreign Office ultimately sought delivery of the survivors to the steamer SAIPAN MARU off Rota, while the State and Navy Departments coordinated the arrangements with the Embassy in Tokyo and Guam authorities.

interest: The sheet is useful as a compact roadmap to a larger body of diplomatic and naval correspondence, even though the underlying papers are not present here. It juxtaposes a deadly mine sinking on the Yangtze near Hankow with the practical diplomacy of repatriating shipwreck survivors in the Japanese-administered Pacific islands. The successive alternatives—Saipan, Guam, and Rota—and the proposed ship-to-ship transfer illustrate how sovereignty, port facilities, and naval coordination shaped even a humanitarian operation. It also preserves the names of several vessels and precise casualty figures that can guide research in related State and Navy Department records.
